title: Most consumer cameras don't capture a frame at once: they scan it line by line

cover.alt: An orange endurance racing car speeds past, its wheels looking like tilted ovals and its body slightly slanted.

body: Most CMOS image sensors in consumer cameras use a **rolling shutter**: instead of recording the whole scene in one instant, they read it out line by line in a rapid sweep. The frame is then shown as if it were a single moment. Anything that moves fast during the sweep is caught at slightly different times in different lines, so race cars lean, propellers bend into odd curves and a camera flash can light just part of the picture. A *global shutter* captures every pixel at the same instant and avoids this.

slides.alt: Race cars flash past a fixed camera beside a track with yellow and blue kerbs; each car looks slanted and its wheels look like tilted ovals.
slides.caption: Le Mans 24 Hours, 2018, filmed on a camera with a CMOS sensor: each passing car looks slanted and its round wheels look like tilted ovals.

slides.prompt: The effect has even been used to steal secret keys from some smart-card readers. How?
slides.answer: By filming the reader's power LED
slides.detail: Each line is read at a different moment, so the video catches the LED's tiny flickers far faster than its frame rate, and those can give the key away.

slides.question: Why does a fast car look slanted in a rolling-shutter video?
options: The lens bends light at speed
Each line is read at a different time
The car really tilts at speed
slides.explanation: The sensor reads line by line, so by the time the last lines are read, the car has moved on. Shown together, the lines make it lean.
